---
title: "Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer"
---

## Today's question

What if a length was entered in the wrong unit, a plant appears twice, or a
measurement is missing? R can calculate a precise-looking answer from a poor
table. Our job is to check what the values mean and leave a record of justified
repairs. Never edit the supplied raw file to make a calculation look convenient.

Today's `data/seedlings-messy.csv` contains deliberately planted errors. Read
[`data/field-notes.txt`](../data/field-notes.txt), which provides the source-record information needed to
resolve them. This is a teaching exercise in verification, not a rule that
unusual observations must be wrong.

## Inspect before converting

Create `day11-cleaning.R` in the project root. Read every column as text so that
mixed entries remain visible. Keep leading/trailing spaces for this inspection.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
raw <- read_csv("data/seedlings-messy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), trim_ws = FALSE)
dim(raw)
unique(raw$treatment)
filter(raw, plant_id %in% c("P01", "P06", "P18", "P21"))
```

`cols(.default = col_character())` requests text columns instead of guessing.
`unique()` shows distinct values, so `"control"` and `"Control"` can be noticed.
`%in%` asks whether a value belongs to the listed set of IDs. A CSV importer may
normally trim surrounding spaces; we temporarily keep them so we can see the
problem rather than mistake automatic tidying for a clean source.

The file has 25 rows although the study has 24 plants. Confirm the duplicated ID:

```{r}
raw |> count(plant_id) |> filter(n > 1)
```

`count()` counts rows by the named column. Repeated IDs can be legitimate if a
table has one row per time point. Here the protocol says one row per plant, so
we inspect both P01 rows and the source record before deciding what to do.

## Make evidence-based repairs

The supplied field notes establish the following:

- The two P01 rows are an accidental duplicate of the same record.
- `Control` means `control`, and a trailing space on a treatment is accidental.
- P18's initial length is 18.7 **mm**; its cell includes the unit as text.
- P21's source record gives final length **43.8 mm**, not the entered 4.38.
- P06's final measurement is unavailable. There is no supported replacement.

The number 4.38 alone would not justify multiplying by ten. The source record
authorises that correction. Similarly, missing P06 is not a length of zero.

```{r}
cleaned <- raw |>
  mutate(treatment = tolower(trimws(treatment)),
         initial_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P18", "18.7", initial_mm),
         final_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P21", "43.8", final_mm)) |>
  distinct() |>
  mutate(initial_mm = parse_double(initial_mm),
         final_mm = parse_double(final_mm),
         growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
```

`trimws()` removes surrounding whitespace, and `tolower()` standardises letters
in these documented labels. `if_else(condition, yes, no)` makes the stated
replacement only for the identified record. `distinct()` removes exact repeated
rows; we use it only after confirming the import duplication. `parse_double()`
turns verified number text into numeric values, preserving missing values.
These are worked repair instructions, not functions to memorise today.

## Check the repaired table

```{r}
nrow(cleaned)
anyDuplicated(cleaned$plant_id)
sum(is.na(cleaned$growth_mm))
cleaned |> count(treatment)
write_csv(cleaned, "output/seedlings-cleaned.csv")
```

Expect 24 rows, zero duplicated IDs, and one missing growth value. Both groups
still contain 12 plants, but the control group has only 11 observed growth values.
Counting enrolled plants and counting usable measurements answer different
questions. Keep the raw file, repair script, and field notes so another person
can trace these decisions.

## Your practical

1. Run the inspection steps before the repair block. Write comments recording
   what prompted each check.
2. Run the repairs and verify the expected counts. Inspect P06, P18, and P21.
3. Calculate the mean of `cleaned$growth_mm` with and without `na.rm = TRUE`.
   Explain what each result means; do not replace the missing value.
4. Save a short `output/cleaning-notes.txt` explaining the evidence for each
   change and the observation left unavailable.
5. Restart R, rerun your script, and confirm the original CSV has 25 rows while
   the derived CSV has 24. Different row counts are expected and documented.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: avoid silently losing records

Inspect `raw |> filter(plant_id == "P01")` before using `distinct()`. Do not use
`distinct(plant_id, .keep_all = TRUE)` to discard different records merely because
they share an ID. Real disagreements need investigation.
:::

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What makes a repair justified?

A check identifies a question; the source record supports the repair. A very
small or large value may be real. Omitting missing values from a calculation
does not make their absence disappear from the report.
:::

**Keep:** `day11-cleaning.R`, the derived CSV, and your cleaning notes.
